metadata.title: Monotonicity and log-behavior of some functions related to the Euler Gamma function

nodes.name: log-concave / log-convex sequence
nodes.statement: Let $\{z_n\}_{n\geq0}$ be a sequence of positive numbers. It is called {\it log-concave} (resp. {\it log-convex}) if $z_{n-1}z_{n+1}\le z_n^2$ (resp. $z_{n-1}z_{n+1}\ge z_n^2$) for all $n\ge 1$. Clearly, the sequence $\{z_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ is log-concave (resp. log-convex) if and only if the sequence $\{z_{n+1}/z_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ is decreasing (resp. increasing).
nodes.statement_short: A positive sequence is log-concave (log-convex) when $z_{n-1}z_{n+1}\le z_n^2$ ($\ge$), equivalently when $z_{n+1}/z_n$ decreases (increases).

nodes.name: Wang and Zhu's monotonicity criterion for $\{\sqrt[n]{z_n}\}$
nodes.statement: For example, for a positive log-convex sequence $\{z_n\}_{n\ge 0}$, if $z_0\le 1$, then the sequence $\{\sqrt[n]{z_n}\}_{n\ge 1}$ is increasing.
nodes.statement_short: A positive log-convex sequence with $z_0\le1$ has increasing $n$-th roots.
conclusions: the sequence $\{\sqrt[n]{z_n}\}_{n\ge 1}$ is increasing

nodes.name: Theorem 1.1 — continuous criterion for strict increase of $\sqrt[x]{f(x)}$
nodes.statement: Let $N$ be a positive number. If $f(x)$ is a positive increasing log-convex function for $x\geq N$ and $f(N)\leq 1$, then $\sqrt[x]{f(x)}$ is strictly increasing on $(N,\infty)$.
nodes.statement_short: A positive increasing log-convex $f$ with $f(N)\le1$ makes $\sqrt[x]{f(x)}$ strictly increasing past $N$.
assumptions: $f(x)$ is a positive increasing log-convex function for $x\geq N$
conclusions: $\sqrt[x]{f(x)}$ is strictly increasing on $(N,\infty)$

nodes.name: Remark 1.2 — applicability of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm+inc} can be applied to the monotonicity of $\{\sqrt[n]{z_n}\}_{n\ge 1}$ for some combinatorial sequences $\{z_n\}_{n\ge 0}$. Some further examples and applications related to Theorem~\ref{thm+inc} can be found in \cite{CGW}.

nodes.name: Example 1.3 — Bernoulli numbers and the function $\theta(x)$
nodes.statement: Recall that the classical Bernoulli numbers are defined by $$B_0=1,\quad \sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n+1}{k}B_k=0,\qquad n=1,2,\ldots.$$ It is well known that $B_{2n+1}=0, (-1)^{n-1}B_{2n}>0$ for $n\ge 1$ and $$(-1)^{n-1}B_{2n}=\frac{2(2n)!\zeta(2n)}{(2\pi)^{2n}},$$ see \cite[(6.89)]{GKP94} for instance. In order to show that $\{\sqrt[n]{(-1)^{n-1}B_{2n}}\}$ is increasing, Chen et al \cite{CGW} introduced the function $\theta(x)=\sqrt[x]{2 \zeta(x)\Gamma(x+1)},$ where $$\zeta(x)=\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{1}{n^x}$$ is the Riemann zeta function and $\Gamma(x)$ is the Euler Gamma function. Thus $$\sqrt[n]{(-1)^{n-1}B_{2n}}={\theta^2(2n)}/{4\pi^{2}}.$$ They proved that $\theta(x)$ is increasing on $(6,\infty)$. In addition, in order to get the log-concavity of $\{\sqrt[n]{(-1)^{n-1}B_{2n}}\}_{n\ge 1}$, they further conjectured.
nodes.statement_short: Recalls the Bernoulli numbers, their zeta formula, and Chen et al.'s function $\theta(x)$ with $\sqrt[n]{(-1)^{n-1}B_{2n}}=\theta^2(2n)/4\pi^2$.

nodes.name: the operator $R$ and infinitely log-monotonic sequences
nodes.statement: define an operator $R$ on a sequence $\{z_n\}_{n\geq 0}$ by $$R\{z_n\}_{n\geq 0}=\{x_n\}_{n\geq 0},$$ where $x_n = z_{n+1}/{z_n}$. The sequence $\{z_n\}_{n\geq 0}$ is called {\it infinitely log-monotonic} if the sequence $R^r\{z_n\}_{n\geq 0}$ is log-concave for all positive odd $r$ and is log-convex for all nonnegative even $r$.
nodes.statement_short: $R$ maps $\{z_n\}$ to its ratio sequence; $\{z_n\}$ is infinitely log-monotonic when every $R^r\{z_n\}$ alternates log-concave/log-convex with the parity of $r$.
differentia: the sequence $R^r\{z_n\}_{n\geq 0}$ is log-concave for all positive odd $r$ and is log-convex for all nonnegative even $r$

nodes.name: completely monotonic function
nodes.statement: Recall that a function $f(x)$ is said to be {\it completely monotonic} on an interval $I$ if $f(x)$ has derivatives of all orders on $I$ which alternate successively in sign, that is, $$(-1)^nf^{(n)}(x)\geq0$$ for all $x\in I$ and for all $n\geq 0$. If inequality is strict for all $x\in I$ and for all $n\geq 0$, then $f(x)$ is said to be strictly completely monotonic.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is completely monotonic on $I$ when $(-1)^nf^{(n)}\geq0$ for all $n$, and strictly so when the inequalities are strict.
differentia: $f(x)$ has derivatives of all orders on $I$ which alternate successively in sign

nodes.name: logarithmically completely monotonic function
nodes.statement: A positive function $f(x)$ is said to be {\it logarithmically completely monotonic} on an interval $I$ if $\log f(x)$ satisfies $$(-1)^n[\log f(x)]^{n}\geq0$$ for all $x\in I$ and for all $n\geq 1$.
differentia: $\log f(x)$ satisfies $$(-1)^n[\log f(x)]^{n}\geq0$$ for all $x\in I$ and for all $n\geq 1$

nodes.name: logarithmically completely monotonic implies completely monotonic
nodes.statement: A logarithmically completely monotonic function is completely monotonic, but not vice versa, see Berg~\cite{Ber04}.
conclusions: is completely monotonic, but not vice versa

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement: \quad Let $y=\sqrt[x]{f(x)}$. Then one can get \begin{equation*} y'=\frac{y}{x}\left(\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}-\frac{\log{f(x)}}{x}\right). \end{equation*} In order to show that $\sqrt[x]{f(x)}$ is strictly increasing, it suffices to prove \begin{equation} \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}-\frac{\log{f(x)}}{x}>0 \end{equation} for $x\geq N$. Since $f(N)\leq 1$ and $f(x)$ is increasing, one can derive that \begin{equation} \frac{\log{f(x)}}{x}\leq\frac{\log{f(x)}-\log{f(N)}}{x}<\frac{\log{f(x)}-\log{f(N)}}{x-N} \end{equation} for $x\geq N$. By the mean value theorem, one can obtain \begin{equation} \frac{\log{f(x)}-\log{f(N)}}{x-N}=\frac{f'(\xi)}{f(\xi)}, \end{equation} where $N\leq\xi\leq x$. On the other hand, it follows from log-convexity of the function $f(x)$ that \begin{equation} \left(\log{f(x)}\right)''=\left(\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\right)'=\frac{f''(x)f(x)-f'(x)^2}{f^2(x)}\geq0, \end{equation} which implies that $\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ is increasing. Thus, it follows that \begin{equation} \frac{f'(\xi)}{f(\xi)}\leq\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} \end{equation} for $x\geq\xi.$ Combining (\ref{e2}), (\ref{e3}) and (\ref{e4}), one can obtain (\ref{e1}). So $\sqrt[x]{f(x)}$ is increasing.

nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} |d_{n}-\frac{n!}{e}|\leq\frac{1}{2} \end{eqnarray} for $n\geq 3$ (see \cite{HSW12})
nodes.statement_short: $|d_n-n!/e|\leq 1/2$ for $n\geq3$.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.6 — asymptotic infinite log-monotonicity of the derangement numbers
nodes.statement: The sequence of the derangements numbers $\{d_n\}_{n\ge 3}$ is asymptotically infinitely log-monotonic.
conclusions: The sequence of the derangements numbers $\{d_n\}_{n\ge 3}$ is asymptotically infinitely log-monotonic

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.6
nodes.statement: From (\ref{e}), one can deduce $$\frac{n!}{e}-\frac{1}{2}\leq d_n\leq \frac{n!}{e}+\frac{1}{2},$$ which implies $$\Gamma(n+1)-\frac{3}{2}\leq e d_n\leq \Gamma(n+1)+\frac{3}{2}.$$ Thus \begin{eqnarray*} &&e^2(d_{n+1}d_{n-1}-d_n^2)\\ &\geq&[\Gamma(n+2)-1.5][\Gamma(n)-1.5]-[\Gamma(n+1)+1.5]^2\\ &>0& \end{eqnarray*} for $n\ge4$, which implies that $\{d_n\}_{n\ge 4}$ is log-convex. Note that \begin{eqnarray*} &&e^4(d_{n+1}^3d_{n-1}-d_{n}^3d_{n+2})\\ &\geq&[\Gamma(n+2)-1.5]^3[\Gamma(n)-1.5]-[\Gamma(n+1)+1.5]^3[\Gamma(n+3)+1.5]\\ &>0& \end{eqnarray*} for $n\ge8$, which implies that $R\{d_n\}_{n\geq 8}$ is log-concave. Because $\{\Gamma(n)\}_{n\geq1}$ is strictly infinitely log-monotonic, similarly, it can be proceeded to the higher order log-monotonicity. Thus, for any positive integer $k $, by the sign-preserving property of limits, one can obtain that there exists a positive $N$ such that the sequence $R^r\{d_n\}_{n\geq N}$ is log-concave for positive odd $r$ and is log-convex for positive even $r$. Thus, the sequence of the derangements numbers $\{d_n\}_{n\ge 3}$ is asymptotically infinitely log-monotonic.
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich $ed_n$ between $\Gamma(n+1)\pm 3/2$, verify log-convexity and ratio log-concavity directly, then push to all orders by the sign-preserving property of limits.

nodes.name: Sandwich $ed_n$ between Gamma values
nodes.statement: From (\ref{e}), one can deduce $$\frac{n!}{e}-\frac{1}{2}\leq d_n\leq \frac{n!}{e}+\frac{1}{2},$$ which implies $$\Gamma(n+1)-\frac{3}{2}\leq e d_n\leq \Gamma(n+1)+\frac{3}{2}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Convert $|d_n-n!/e|\leq1/2$ into $\Gamma(n+1)-3/2\leq ed_n\leq\Gamma(n+1)+3/2$.

nodes.name: Log-convexity for $n\geq4$
nodes.statement: Thus \begin{eqnarray*} &&e^2(d_{n+1}d_{n-1}-d_n^2)\\ &\geq&[\Gamma(n+2)-1.5][\Gamma(n)-1.5]-[\Gamma(n+1)+1.5]^2\\ &>0& \end{eqnarray*} for $n\ge4$, which implies that $\{d_n\}_{n\ge 4}$ is log-convex.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $e^2(d_{n+1}d_{n-1}-d_n^2)$ below by a positive Gamma expression for $n\geq4$.

nodes.name: Ratio log-concavity for $n\geq8$
nodes.statement: Note that \begin{eqnarray*} &&e^4(d_{n+1}^3d_{n-1}-d_{n}^3d_{n+2})\\ &\geq&[\Gamma(n+2)-1.5]^3[\Gamma(n)-1.5]-[\Gamma(n+1)+1.5]^3[\Gamma(n+3)+1.5]\\ &>0& \end{eqnarray*} for $n\ge8$, which implies that $R\{d_n\}_{n\geq 8}$ is log-concave.
nodes.statement_short: The analogous fourth-order estimate shows $R\{d_n\}$ is log-concave for $n\geq8$.

nodes.name: Iterate to all orders by limits
nodes.statement: Because $\{\Gamma(n)\}_{n\geq1}$ is strictly infinitely log-monotonic, similarly, it can be proceeded to the higher order log-monotonicity. Thus, for any positive integer $k $, by the sign-preserving property of limits, one can obtain that there exists a positive $N$ such that the sequence $R^r\{d_n\}_{n\geq N}$ is log-concave for positive odd $r$ and is log-convex for positive even $r$. Thus, the sequence of the derangements numbers $\{d_n\}_{n\ge 3}$ is asymptotically infinitely log-monotonic.
nodes.statement_short: Infinite log-monotonicity of $\Gamma$ plus the sign-preserving property of limits extends the argument to every order.

nodes.name: the function $\theta_{a,b,c}(x)=\sqrt[x]{a \zeta(x+b)\Gamma(x+c)}$
nodes.statement: In order to consider a stronger result for Theorem~\ref{thm+con}, given $a,b,c>0$, define the function $$\theta_{a,b,c}(x)=\sqrt[x]{a \zeta(x+b)\Gamma(x+c)}.$$

nodes.name: complete monotonicity of $\zeta$ and of $[\log\Gamma]''$
nodes.statement: It is known that the Riemann zeta function $\zeta(x)$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(1,+\infty)$ and the function $[\log\Gamma(x)]^{''}$ is completely monotonic on $(0,+\infty)$, see Chen {\it et al.} \cite{CGW1}.
conclusions: the Riemann zeta function $\zeta(x)$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(1,+\infty)$
the function $[\log\Gamma(x)]^{''}$ is completely monotonic on $(0,+\infty)$

nodes.name: Theorem 4.7 — logarithmic complete monotonicity of $1/\theta_{a,b,c}(x)$
nodes.statement: Let $a,b,c$ be positive real numbers, where $b\geq 1$. If $a\zeta(b)\Gamma(c)\leq1$, then the reciprocal of the function $\theta_{a,b,c}(x)$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(1,\infty)$.
assumptions: Let $a,b,c$ be positive real numbers, where $b\geq 1$
conclusions: the reciprocal of the function $\theta_{a,b,c}(x)$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(1,\infty)$

nodes.name: derivative formula for $g(x)/x$
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \left(\frac{g(x)}{x}\right)^{(n)}=\frac{(-1)^ng(0)n!}{x^{n+1}}+x^{-n-1}\int_0^x t^n g^{(n+1)}(x)dt, \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: $(g(x)/x)^{(n)}$ equals $(-1)^ng(0)n!/x^{n+1}$ plus an integral of $t^ng^{(n+1)}$.
nodes.origin_citation: stated as a known formula, provable by induction (no citation given)

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.7
nodes.statement: Since $$\log\theta^{-1}_{a,b,c}(x)=-\frac{\log\left(a\zeta(x+b)\Gamma(x+c)\right)}{x}=-\frac{\log a+\log\zeta(x+b)+\log\Gamma(x+c)}{x},$$ in order to show that $\theta^{-1}_{a,b,c}(x)$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(1,\infty)$, it suffices to prove $$(-1)^n\log^{(n)}\theta^{-1}_{a,b,c}(x)\geq0$$ for all $n\geq1$. Note that a known formula as follows: \begin{eqnarray} \left(\frac{g(x)}{x}\right)^{(n)}=\frac{(-1)^ng(0)n!}{x^{n+1}}+x^{-n-1}\int_0^x t^n g^{(n+1)}(x)dt, \end{eqnarray} which can be easily proved by induction. Thus, one can deduce for $n\geq1$ and $x>1$ that \begin{eqnarray*} &&(-1)^n\log^{(n)}\theta^{-1}_{a,b,c}(x)\\ &&=\frac{-n!\log{a\zeta(b)\Gamma(c)}}{x^{n+1}}+x^{-n-1}\int_0^x t^n (-1)^{n+1}\left[\left(\log\zeta(x+b)\right)^{(n+1)}+\left(\log\Gamma(x+c)\right)^{(n+1)}\right]dt\\ &&\geq0 \end{eqnarray*} since $\log{a\zeta(b)\Gamma(c)}\leq0$, $(-1)^{n+1}\left(\log\zeta(x+b)\right)^{(n+1)}\geq0$ and $(-1)^{n+1}\left(\log\Gamma(x+c)\right)^{(n+1)}\geq0$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\log\theta^{-1}$ as $-(\log a+\log\zeta+\log\Gamma)/x$ and apply the derivative formula (4.5) together with complete monotonicity of $\log\zeta$ and $\log\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Reduce to the sign of $(-1)^n\log^{(n)}\theta^{-1}_{a,b,c}$
nodes.statement: Since $$\log\theta^{-1}_{a,b,c}(x)=-\frac{\log\left(a\zeta(x+b)\Gamma(x+c)\right)}{x}=-\frac{\log a+\log\zeta(x+b)+\log\Gamma(x+c)}{x},$$ in order to show that $\theta^{-1}_{a,b,c}(x)$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(1,\infty)$, it suffices to prove $$(-1)^n\log^{(n)}\theta^{-1}_{a,b,c}(x)\geq0$$ for all $n\geq1$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\log\theta^{-1}_{a,b,c}$ and reduce to $(-1)^n\log^{(n)}\theta^{-1}_{a,b,c}(x)\geq0$.

nodes.name: Invoke the derivative formula for $g(x)/x$
nodes.statement: Note that a known formula as follows: \begin{eqnarray} \left(\frac{g(x)}{x}\right)^{(n)}=\frac{(-1)^ng(0)n!}{x^{n+1}}+x^{-n-1}\int_0^x t^n g^{(n+1)}(x)dt, \end{eqnarray} which can be easily proved by induction.
nodes.statement_short: Quote the formula for $(g(x)/x)^{(n)}$, provable by induction.

nodes.name: Conclude nonnegativity
nodes.statement: Thus, one can deduce for $n\geq1$ and $x>1$ that \begin{eqnarray*} &&(-1)^n\log^{(n)}\theta^{-1}_{a,b,c}(x)\\ &&=\frac{-n!\log{a\zeta(b)\Gamma(c)}}{x^{n+1}}+x^{-n-1}\int_0^x t^n (-1)^{n+1}\left[\left(\log\zeta(x+b)\right)^{(n+1)}+\left(\log\Gamma(x+c)\right)^{(n+1)}\right]dt\\ &&\geq0 \end{eqnarray*} since $\log{a\zeta(b)\Gamma(c)}\leq0$, $(-1)^{n+1}\left(\log\zeta(x+b)\right)^{(n+1)}\geq0$ and $(-1)^{n+1}\left(\log\Gamma(x+c)\right)^{(n+1)}\geq0$.
nodes.statement_short: Both terms are nonnegative because $\log a\zeta(b)\Gamma(c)\leq0$ and $\log\zeta$, $\log\Gamma$ have completely monotonic derivatives.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.8 of Alzer — complete monotonicity of $\prod\Gamma(x+a_i)/\Gamma(x+b_i)$
nodes.statement: Let nonnegative sequences $0\leq a_1\leq a_2\leq a_3\leq\cdots\leq a_n$ and $0\leq b_1\leq b_2\leq b_3\leq\cdots\leq b_n$. If $\sum_{i=1}^ka_i\leq \sum_{i=1}^kb_i$ for $k=1,2,\ldots,n$, then the function $$\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(x+a_i)}{\Gamma(x+b_i)}$$ is completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$.
nodes.statement_short: Majorization of the partial sums of $(a_i)$ by those of $(b_i)$ makes the Gamma-ratio product completely monotonic.
assumptions: Let nonnegative sequences $0\leq a_1\leq a_2\leq a_3\leq\cdots\leq a_n$ and $0\leq b_1\leq b_2\leq b_3\leq\cdots\leq b_n$
conclusions: the function $$\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(x+a_i)}{\Gamma(x+b_i)}$$ is completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$

nodes.name: Lee and Tepedelenlioglu's logarithmically completely monotonic coding-gain function
nodes.statement: On the other hand, in \cite{LT11}, Lee and Tepedelenlio\v{g}lu proved the function $\sqrt[x]{\frac{2\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(x+1)}{\Gamma(x+1/2)}}$ originating from the coding gain is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$.
conclusions: the function $\sqrt[x]{\frac{2\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(x+1)}{\Gamma(x+1/2)}}$ originating from the coding gain is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$

nodes.name: Theorem 4.9 — logarithmic complete monotonicity of $\chi(x)=\sqrt[x]{\rho\prod\Gamma(x+a_i)/\Gamma(x+b_i)}$
nodes.statement: Let $0\leq a_1\leq a_2\leq a_3\leq\cdots\leq a_n$, $0\leq b_1\leq b_2\leq b_3\leq\cdots\leq b_n$ and $\rho>0$, define the function $$\chi(x)=\sqrt[x]{\rho\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(x+a_i)}{\Gamma(x+b_i)}}.$$ \begin{itemize} \item [\rm (i)] If $\rho\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(a_i)}{\Gamma(b_i)}\geq1$ and $\sum_{i=1}^ka_i\geq \sum_{i=1}^kb_i$ for $k=1,2,\ldots,n$, then the function $\chi(x)$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$. \item [\rm (ii)] If $\rho\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(a_i)}{\Gamma(b_i)}\leq1$ and $\sum_{i=1}^ka_i\leq \sum_{i=1}^kb_i$ for $k=1,2,\ldots,n$, then the reciprocal of the function $\chi(x)$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Under matching majorization and a normalization at $x=0$, either $\chi$ or its reciprocal is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$.
assumptions: Let $0\leq a_1\leq a_2\leq a_3\leq\cdots\leq a_n$, $0\leq b_1\leq b_2\leq b_3\leq\cdots\leq b_n$ and $\rho>0$
conclusions: the function $\chi(x)$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$
the reciprocal of the function $\chi(x)$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.9
nodes.statement: Because (ii) can be obtained in the similar way, it only needs to prove (i). Define the function $h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log \Gamma(x+a_i)-\log\Gamma(x+b_i)$. Then $$\log\sqrt[x]{\rho\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(x+a_i)}{\Gamma(x+b_i)}}=\frac{\log\rho\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(x+a_i)}{\Gamma(x+b_i)}}{x} =\frac{\log\rho+h(x)}{x}.$$ So it is not hard to get \begin{eqnarray} &&(-1)^k[\log\chi(x)]^{(k)}=\frac{k!(\log\rho+h(0))}{x^{k+1}}+x^{-k-1}\int_0^x t^k (-1)^kh^{(k+1)}(x)dt. \end{eqnarray} If $\rho\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(a_i)}{\Gamma(b_i)}\geq1$, then it is clear that $$\log\rho+h(0)\geq0.$$ In addition, Alzer \cite{Al97} proved that $(-1)^kh^{(k+1)}(x)\geq0$ for $k\geq0$ and $x\geq0$. Thus, $$(-1)^k[\log\chi(x)]^{(k)}\geq0,$$ that is, $\chi(x)$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\log\chi=(\log\rho+h(x))/x$, expand its derivatives with the $g(x)/x$ formula, and use $\log\rho+h(0)\geq0$ plus Alzer's sign result.

nodes.name: Reduce to part (i) and set up $h(x)$
nodes.statement: Because (ii) can be obtained in the similar way, it only needs to prove (i). Define the function $h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log \Gamma(x+a_i)-\log\Gamma(x+b_i)$. Then $$\log\sqrt[x]{\rho\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(x+a_i)}{\Gamma(x+b_i)}}=\frac{\log\rho\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(x+a_i)}{\Gamma(x+b_i)}}{x} =\frac{\log\rho+h(x)}{x}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Only (i) needs proof; define $h(x)=\sum_i(\log\Gamma(x+a_i)-\log\Gamma(x+b_i))$ so $\log\chi=(\log\rho+h)/x$.

nodes.name: Expand the $k$-th derivative of $\log\chi$
nodes.statement: So it is not hard to get \begin{eqnarray} &&(-1)^k[\log\chi(x)]^{(k)}=\frac{k!(\log\rho+h(0))}{x^{k+1}}+x^{-k-1}\int_0^x t^k (-1)^kh^{(k+1)}(x)dt. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the $g(x)/x$ derivative formula to $(-1)^k[\log\chi(x)]^{(k)}$.

nodes.name: Sign both terms
nodes.statement: If $\rho\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(a_i)}{\Gamma(b_i)}\geq1$, then it is clear that $$\log\rho+h(0)\geq0.$$ In addition, Alzer \cite{Al97} proved that $(-1)^kh^{(k+1)}(x)\geq0$ for $k\geq0$ and $x\geq0$.
nodes.statement_short: The normalization gives $\log\rho+h(0)\geq0$ and Alzer's result gives $(-1)^kh^{(k+1)}\geq0$.

nodes.name: Conclude logarithmic complete monotonicity
nodes.statement: Thus, $$(-1)^k[\log\chi(x)]^{(k)}\geq0,$$ that is, $\chi(x)$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$.
nodes.statement_short: Both terms nonnegative gives $(-1)^k[\log\chi(x)]^{(k)}\geq0$.

nodes.name: Remark 4.10 — Theorem 4.9 generalizes Lee-Tepedelenlioglu and Qi-Li
nodes.statement: If $\rho=2\sqrt{\pi}$, $a_1=1$ and $b_1=\frac{1}{2}$, then $\frac{2\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(1)}{\Gamma(1/2)}=2>1$. So the function $\sqrt[x]{\frac{2\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(x+1)}{\Gamma(x+1/2)}}$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$, see \cite{LT11}. In addition, if $n=1$ in Theorem~\ref{thm+comp}, then it was proved by Qi and Li \cite{QL13}. Thus, the result in Theorem~\ref{thm+comp} is a generalization.
nodes.statement_short: Specializing $\rho=2\sqrt{\pi}$, $a_1=1$, $b_1=1/2$ recovers Lee-Tepedelenlioglu, and $n=1$ recovers Qi-Li.
